title: Protective behavioral strategies for psychedelic use: A mini review of the evidence

claims.statement: In adults who have used classic psychedelics, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything people do during a difficult experience makes it shorter or easier: no study read here tested a way of coping, and what is known is what people say helped, looking back, on which two independent surveys agree. In a self-selected online survey of 529 people recalling a challenging experience with psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline (Wood et al., 2024), the responses, of 26 listed, most often tried and judged helpful were letting go, accepting or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%); the least often were directing anger at the experience (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling it to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%). People who judged more acceptance-type responses helpful rated their emotional breakthrough higher (r = 0.50), but both were rated at one sitting, sometimes years later, and judging a response helpful may itself reflect how the experience ended. Sixteen people who had attended psilocybin retreats, chosen because their difficult ceremonies had been followed by personal change, wrote of breathing on purpose, opening their eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, and facilitators' touch, listening and reminders to breathe; one found evasive reassurance unhelpful. In a US online panel, 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience, ticked what had helped during their most challenging one: trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%), changing location 168 (27.4%), asking a friend for help 124 (20.2%), changing the people around 124 (20.2%) and changing the music 99 (16.2%); fewer ticked taking another drug (smoking cannabis 113, 18.4%; drinking alcohol 54, 8.8%; another drug 22, 3.6%), which, like every other response, no study tested (Simonsson et al., 2023). As summarized second-hand in a mini review (Piercey et al., 2024), 91% of respondents to an earlier survey of difficult experiences with psilocybin mushrooms used at least one such strategy and rated them only modestly effective, and 65.9% of surveyed callers to a psychedelic peer-support phone line said it helped ease their distress. None of these studies compared people who did something with people who did not. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: No effect estimates. Tried and judged helpful (Wood et al., 2024; n = 529): letting go 84.5%, observing the mind 77.3%, closing the eyes or lying down 73.9%; least often anger 9.4%, trying to sleep 9.7%, telling it to stop 10.6%, another drug or alcohol 12.1%. Ticked as helpful (Simonsson et al., 2023; n = 613): calming the mind 41.9%, changing location 27.4%, asking a friend 20.2%, changing the people around 20.2%, changing the music 16.2%, cannabis 18.4%, alcohol 8.8%, another drug 3.6%. Second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024): 91% used strategies, rated modestly effective; 65.9% of helpline callers found it helpful.

claims.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy, evidence is insufficient to say whether harm reduction habits lower the chance of a difficult experience. The one survey that measured both (Palmer and Maynard, 2022; pre-registered) asked 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people (median 11.5 lifetime uses), reached through university societies and online psychedelic communities, to recall their first experience (a median of 42 months earlier) and their most recent one (a median of 2 months earlier): which listed practices they had used before, during and after, how challenging it had been (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) and how much emotional breakthrough it brought (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory). A score adding up the practices each person used, each weighted by how important the sample rated it for safety, correlated weakly with lower challenge for the first experience (r = −0.21, 95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) and not significantly for the most recent (r = −0.15, −0.30 to 0.00), and with more breakthrough on both occasions (r = 0.24, 0.09 to 0.38), 2 to 6% of the variation (editors' intervals and calculation). The score counted practices after the experience, which cannot have shaped it, was weighted by the respondents' own judgments, was recalled at the same sitting as the outcomes and was not adjusted for anything, and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. Scores were higher for the most recent experience (48.7 against 40.1), for practices before and after use but not during it, while challenge scores did not change (17.1 and 17.3% of the maximum). Most were with trusted friends, a practice they rated important; few had a sober sitter, which they rated low; and few tested their drugs, although they rated testing as important. In a US online panel, 182 of 613 people (29.7%) blamed a lack of preparation for their most challenging experience, which went with slightly higher challenge ratings (beta 0.09) but not with later thoughts of harm (adjusted odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.45) (Simonsson et al., 2023). A mini review that rests largely on the first survey summarizes it as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, which overstates it; the review adds a catalogue of strategies named in the literature and finds outcome research scarce: for classic psychedelics, that survey and one preparedness-scale study, and for ketamine and MDMA, one survey and one unreviewed preprint, all second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163: importance-weighted practice score and challenge r = −0.21 (95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) for the first experience, −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00) for the most recent; with breakthrough r = 0.24 (0.09 to 0.38) on both (editors' intervals; 2% to 6% of the variation). Score 40.06 first against 48.68 most recent; challenge 17.14 against 17.29 per cent of the maximum. Simonsson et al.
